title: ‘No indications’ PHP code flaw has led to government systems being hacked, cyber security official says – UK politics live
text:
Cyber security official says there are 'no indications' PHP code flaw has led to government computer systems being hacked
Ollie Whitehouse, chief technology officer at the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, told Radio 4’s the World at One that incidents like today’s computer system shutdowns because of a coding problem were likely to re-occur. He explained:
[This] highlights to a lot of organisations that technology is not a one-time purchase now, that it needs that continuous investment throughout its operational lifetime.
We’re in an era now of digital dependency, coupled with heightened cyber threat, coupled with increasing capability, which means all organisations are going to likely have to revisit their risk assumptions and work out how they are able to invest in technology to be able to meet the contemporary era.
Whitehouse said there were “no indications” that the PHP flaw now being fixed had been successfully exploited by hackers.
He also said that the problem that had led to 32 government websites being temporarily shut down (see 12.54pm) was originally identified months ago. He said the NCSC had been conducting a “coordinated disclosure process” to warn organisations of the vulnerability, until a leak meant that the process had to be accelerated.
A UK cyber security official has said that there are “no indications” that the PHP computer coding flaw, that has led to 32 government websites being taken down, has been successfully exploited by hackers. (See 4.46pm.)
MPs pay tribute to Diane Abbott as they debate black history month
MPs debated black history month earlier today. Politicians are often fairly unpleasant to their opponents, but there was a surprise moment near the start of the debate when Joy Morrissey, the Tory spokesperson for women and equalities (and not someone known for being particularly woke or leftwing), paid a moving tribute to the veteran Labour MP Diane Abbott. Morrissey said:
In 1987, the very same year black history month began here, a young woman from Paddington walked into the House of Commons as Britain’s first black female MP. Today, she is the mother of the House.
When she arrived, there were only 41 women in the entire Commons. She was told in a hundred ways that she didn’t belong. She stayed anyway.
For nearly four decades, she has represented the people of Hackney, championed black children in London schools, and chaired parliamentary groups on West Indian and sickle cell disease.
She has faced more abuse than almost any politician of her generation, and she has never stopped turning up.
You don’t have to share her political her politics to recognise what her presence meant. For millions of black Britons, especially black girls, she was proof that the doors of power could open and that someone who looked like them could walk through.
Florence Eshalomi, the communities minister, opened the debate, and she also paid tribute to Abbott. She said she remembered when Abbott was elected in 1987, along with Paul Boateng and Bernie Grant. They were the first black MPs. Eshalomi said:
I was just six years old when [Abbott] was elected, and I remember that quiet hope I felt in watching TV and seeing her in parliament to see that, yes, a black woman can have that voice and that we don’t have to stand by when decisions are made to us and not by us. That gave me the confidence to stand for public office as a local councillor in the borough where I grew up, and later for the London assembly.
Voters significantly more likely to back progressive coalition led by Burnham than Tory/Reform UK one, poll suggests
YouGov has published some interesting polling on what voters think about various coalition options. Here are some of the key points.
Voters are significantly more likely to support a progressive coalition than a rightwing coalition. The most popular coalition option polled was a Labour/Lib Dem one, with Andy Burnham as PM. Some 42% of people would support that. Other progressive options, with Burnham as PM, would get the support of more than a third of voters. But only a quarter of voters would back a Conservative/Reform UK coalition, with a Kemi Badenoch-led version only marginally more popular than a Nigel Farage-led one.
Conservative supporters would rather see the party go into coalition with the Liberal Democrats than with Reform UK. In its write-up, YouGov says:
Most current Conservative supporters would support either arrangement, though more are in favour of the party forming a coalition with the Lib Dems (68%) than Reform (60%), and with at least 28% opposed to either coalition. Lib Dem supporters do not return the favour, with 58% of those currently intending to vote for the party opposed to a repeat of the Cameron-Clegg government, although 36% are in favour.
This is interesting because, on immigration, Brexit, and the European convention on human rights, Badenoch has shifted her party to a position where its policies are near identical to Reform UK’s. Recently there have been signs she has started to steer back the other way.
Most Conservative supporters would not be in favour of a coalition with Reform UK, with Nigel Farage as PM, if the two parties combined could form a majority government. In December last year Conservative supporters (defined as people who voted Tory in 2024) were narrowly in favour of this option. They would still favour a Conservative-Reform UK coalition if Badenoch were PM, but by a narrower margin than last year. YouGov says:
Britons have become less inclined towards a Farage-led Reform-Tory coalition, with net support for such a government falling from -27 to -41 since last December. This includes 2024 Conservative voters going from being effectively divided on the question (+5) to being clearly opposed (-13).
Conservative voters have also become less receptive to a Badenoch-led Tory-Reform coalition, with net support falling 15 points since the end of last year to +23, even if those who voted Reform at the last election have become more open to the idea, with net support doubling to +22.
Fahnbulleh says ministers won't 'faff around' in getting rid of gas standing charges, implying decision coming in budget
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, has heightened speculation that a government announcement about getting rid of the standing charges on gas bills will come in the budget on Wednesday next week.
Andy Burnham implied this strongly yesterday when he said he had asked John Healey, the chancellor, and Fahnbulleh to look at this idea and to report back to MPs “at the earliest opportunity”. The “earliest opportunity” is Wednesday next week, because that will be the first time either of those two MPs gets to address the Commons.
Today, speaking to a press gallery lunch, Fahnbulleh confirmed that an announcement is likely very soon. She said Burnham had made it clear the government “can’t faff around”.
She explained:
I love working with him because Andy is very clear … in his mind about the sorts of things that he wants us to do, and he’s really impatient with change.
And so, if you ask the department, ‘Oh, you know, standing charge reform’, they’re like, ‘Oh, we’d have to consult. This is a 10-year proposition’. And Andy’s like, ‘I want you and John to look at it and come back with an answer’. So we’re looking at the options.
Fahnbulleh said getting rid of standing charges would be popular.
The thing I do know is that the public absolutely hates standing charges, and it’s a control question. People just find that really egregious, and their ability to manage their energy bills by deciding how much they want to use on their terms is essentially taken away from them. So, even shifting it into the unit rate gives people that agency.
She said modelling suggested the move could reduce the bills of “a big stack of low-income through to middle-income households”.
She went on:
There are some people that will be impacted negatively because they are essentially low-income, high users, and so you need to think about mitigations. But we’re looking at all the options.
But the thing that he is very clear on is we can’t faff around. We need to get on with this. So watch this space.
According to research by Nesta, a research foundation, 64% of households would benefit if the government got rid of the standing charge and instead loaded those costs onto the unit charge. But households using large amounts of gas would pay more.
Our analysis shows that, on its own, abolishing the gas standing charge would save the typical dual fuel household £27 per year, and that 64% of dual fuel households will be better off under this policy.
Because the distribution of gas consumption is skewed by a small number of (predominantly wealthy) households, the average and median household are quite a way apart. The threshold at which this policy would start to increase bills is around 12,400 kWh, but a majority of homes (64%) use less gas than this. This is why the typical household (using only 9,500 kWh of gas) would expect to save around £27 per year under this policy.
TDCV stands for typical domestic consumption values – a figure for how much gas and electricity an average household is using at any point.
Burnham has flu jab, as NHS encourages those eligible for free injection to get one
Andy Burnham has had his flu jab. He has posted about it on Instagram, and at the same time the Department of Health and Social Care is launching a publicity campaign to encourage people eligible for a free jab to get one.
James Frith, a health minister, said:
Vaccines save lives. It has never been easier to find out if you are eligible and get vaccinated, helping protect yourself and reduce pressure on the NHS during the winter season.
Eligibility is focused on those most vulnerable - from young children to older adults and people with long-term health conditions - so if you are eligible, please come forward this winter.
In England, most children under 17 are eligible for a free flu jab, as well as people over 65, people with some long-term health conditions, pregnant women, carers and people living in a care home, people living with someone with a weakened immune system, homeless people and frontline health and care workers.
The latest edition of the Guardian’s Politics Weekly UK podcast is out. It features Jessica Elgot and Alexandra Topping talking about whether or not the government will allow the Rosebank oilfield development to go ahead, after the less controversial Jackdaw gasfield was approved yesterday.
Starmer granted core participant status in grooming gangs inquiry
Keir Starmer may be summoned to give evidence at the grooming gangs inquiry, the Press Association reports. PA says:
The former prime minister, who ordered the probe last year, has been listed as a core participant for the inquiry’s hearings which are due to begin in December.
This means he is among people, groups and organisations formally granted special status by the chairwoman under public inquiry rules, giving him rights to participate in the investigation.
While this does not automatically mean he will be required to give evidence, many core participants are asked or compelled to do so.
Victims and their families, charities, whistleblowers, police chiefs and government departments are among those also listed as core participants.
The scandal-hit probe is looking at how grooming gangs operated in England and Wales and the actions of police, councils, health and social care services, schools and other public bodies.
An inquiry spokesman said the decision on core participant status “considers whether a person played, or may have played, a direct and significant role in relation to the matters to which the inquiry relates, whether they have a significant interest in an important aspect of the matters to which the inquiry relates, or whether the person may be subject to explicit or significant criticism during the inquiry proceedings or in the report, or in any interim report”, adding: “Nobody is beyond examination or transparency, and that the inquiry is following the evidence, wherever it leads.”
Starmer was prime minister when the grooming gangs inquiry was announced last year. But he was also director of public prosecutions from 2008 to 2013, at a time when the CPS was being accused of being too reluctant to prosecute in many cases of alleged child sexual abuse. As DPP, Starmer set out to change this – ordering prosecutors to be more sympathetic to victims, and less inclined to disbelieve them or to drop cases because victims might not make compelling witnesses.
According to Christopher Hope from GB News, Kemi Badenoch is unhappy about Andy Burnham going on Gogglebox (see 2.35pm) – but only because she wants an invite too! Hope says:
A political row has broken out over Andy Burnham’s decision to go on Channel 4’s programme ‘Gogglebox’. A Tory source tells me that Kemi Badenoch should be invited on to the show. One says: “It’s Channel 4’s job to ensure political balance.”

Burnham to appear on Gogglebox with Steve Rotheram
Kemi Badenoch has been routinely complaining about Andy Burnham spending time on supposedly trivial things, like discussing how he makes his tea in a summer Q&A, or doing a social media video about pork scratchings. So God know what she is going to say when she finds out he’s on Gogglebox tomorrow night.
The PM will be appearing on the show tomorrow night for a Gogglebox for Stand Up To Cancer special. He will be on the sofa with his friend Steve Rotheram, the Liverpool city region mayor.
As Max Goldbart writes in an article for Deadline, there is some precedent for his appearance.
Seen as something of an everyman, Burnham will now get the chance to broadcast his thoughts on the week’s TV to millions. An Instagram reel teasing his appearance shows him offering crisps and beer to Rotheram.
Burnham is the first prime minister to appear on Gogglebox. Jeremy Corbyn, who was leader of the opposition at the time, came on the show a decade ago, while former PM Boris Johnson’s father Stanley Johnson appeared two years later.
“Nearly 7,000 miles of road resurfacing – the equivalent of travelling between London and Singapore – will be completed this year,” the Department for Transportis saying. It says councils in England are doing 10% more resurfacing than last year, because they are getting more government funding.
Mahmood condemned by Unison for refusing to let care worker attend private meeting about her 'nasty' proposed ILR changes
Andrea Egan, the Unison general secretary, has criticised Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, for not letting her bring a care worker to a meeting to discuss Mahmood’s plans to tighten the permanent residency rules for foreign workers.
Egan described the proposals as “nasty”, and said Mahmood’s failure to engage with people affected by the rules was “totally unacceptable”.
The Unison leader was commenting in a post on social media that referenced a story by Arj Singh for the i, which said talks between Mahmood and Unison “broke down after the home secretary refused to allow a migrant care worker to attend the meeting”. Singh said:
The meeting was cancelled by Unison after Mahmood refused Egan’s late request to bring a migrant care worker who will be affected by the “earned settlement” changes, The i Paper understands.
Mahmood is under pressure to water down her proposals, particularly those relating to care workers, and Unison, which represents many workers in the care sector, has campaigned particularly forcefully against the plan.
In her social media posts, Egan said:
Shabana Mahmood’s failure to engage properly with the migrant workers whose lives her nasty proposals will devastate is totally unacceptable.
These are brilliant, committed workers who hold our public services together. UNISON won’t tolerate them being attacked and ignored.
I’ve changed UNISON’s political approach to put members first. That includes taking members with me to government meetings.
Engaging directly with workers should be standard for Labour cabinet ministers, not something they run away from.
In his report, Singh says:
The care worker who Egan wanted to bring to the meeting has completed an NVQ level 3 and is set to do further qualifications so that he can develop his career in the sector, and was planning to tell Mahmood about why he and many other Unison members had chosen to work in the sector.
Singh quotes a Home Office source as saying that Egan had been invited to a private meeting with Mahmood and that it was Unison that chose to cancel it. The source also said that it would be wrong for Mahmood to prioritise the views of just one care worker when 200,000 responses to the government’s consultation were being considered.
In a social media post commenting on the same story, the Labour MP John McDonnell said:
The work visa issue is causing totally unnecessary division in the Labour Party at a time when the new leader is settling himself into the job. Listening to numerous workers employed on work visas in the care sector has been essential in gaining an understanding of what they face and the effect on our public services of the proposed rule changes. All Unison wanted was to ensure the home secretary had the opportunity to appreciate fully the concerns of the people who will be affected by her proposals. I urge her to think again on this decision not to meet.
32 UK government services offline while work carried out to sort out PHP programming flaw, minister says
Some 32 government services are offline and four are partially unavailable while work is carried out to address potential cybersecurity issues, a minister has said.
As the Press Association reports, organisations around the world have been scrambling to fix a critical security flaw in the programming language PHP used by the majority of websites.
Downing Street on Thursday said no large UK public-facing critical services have been affected, but some “limited” government websites have gone dark while issues are resolved. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) experts are working with OpenAI, whose technology was used to discover the vulnerabilities, and partners around the globe to address potential problems, a No 10 spokesperson said.
In the House of Lords, Liz Lloyd, the tech minister, said:
The information I have is that 32 government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable.
Lloyd said that “has largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied”.
The No 10 spokesperson told reporters:
Work has already taken place across government to identify and fix potential exposures to our systems, and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue.
Here is our story about the global impact of the problems identified in the PHP programming language. It’s by Robert Booth and Aisha Down.
Steve Witkoff wrong about Putin being a 'humanitarian', says No 10
Yesterday Steve Witkoff, the property developer appointed by Donald Trump as his lead foreign policy envoy, described Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian”. Andrew Roth has more about that here, in a piece pointing out that this is an extraordinary lie.
Douglas Alexander, the Scottish secretary, was giving interviews this morning. Asked if he agreed with Witkoff’s description on LBC, he was reassuringly blunt. He replied:
No, we don’t.
We see him as somebody who illegally invaded Ukraine at the start of this conflict, who has been responsible for conduct by his government that included attempted assassinations on UK soil.
So we simply do not recognise the description of Vladimir Putin as a humanitarian.
In contrast, we are crystal clear that we stand foursquare behind Volodymyr Zelensky and the people of Ukraine in their battle for freedom.
At the No 10 lobby briefing, a No 10 spokesperson also argued that Witkoff had got it wrong. Asked about Witkoff’s comment, the spokesperson said:
We do not recognise that characterisation … Putin has killed thousands of people, Ukrainians and his own. He’s starving children and the elderly of heat and warmth and destroying critical national infrastructure.
Tories claim crime figures 'spiralling out of control' - and why the data doesn't back this up
The Conservative party seems to have missed the bit in the ONS report on the crime figures where it said “crime against individuals and households has generally decreased over the last 10 years”. (See 9.54am.) Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, has issued a statement saying:
Crime is spiralling out of control under Labour. Record numbers of sexual offences, knife crime and shop theft show what happens when criminals know they can get away with it. This is a direct consequence of Labour cutting police numbers by 2,000 and letting thousands of prisoners out of jail early.
The Tories justify this claim by looking at the ONS report and picking out all the worst bits (a technique not unfamiliar in the world of journalism). Their briefing highlights four figures in particular. Here is an extract.
Sexual offences have reached the highest level on record under Labour, with the police now logging around 600 of them every single day. Police in England and Wales recorded 218,994 sexual offences in the year to June 2026, the highest annual total since the series began in 2002-03 …
Police are recording more rapes of women than at any point since records began, at a rate of around 142 every day. There were 51,731 recorded rapes of women aged 16 or over in the year to June 2026, the highest figure since the series began in 2004-05 …
More people are being caught carrying knives and blades than at any point since records began. Police recorded 30,216 offences of possessing an article with a blade or point in the year to June 2026, the highest figure since the series began in 2008-09 …
Thefts and robberies from shops have reached a record high under Labour, with more than 1,500 recorded every single day. Police recorded 519,516 shoplifting offences and 31,089 robberies of business property in the year to June 2026, a combined 550,605 and the highest total since the series began in 2002-03.
But these claims are highly selective – to the point of being misleading.
On sexual offences, and rape, the ONS report points out that much of the increase over time is due to more offences being recorded, and not necessarily more of them taking place. It says “there has been a general increase in police recorded sexual offences over the last decade, largely because of improvements in police recording practices”. And it includes a specific warning about drawing the wrong conclusions from the figures.
Police recorded sexual offences are not a good indicator of trends over time. Improvements in police recording practices, the introduction of new offences, and increased reporting by victims have contributed to the level of offences in recent years.
On knives, while more people may be carrying them, the Tories have ignored the figures suggesting fewer criminals are actually using them. The ONS says:
Knife-enabled crime recorded by the police decreased by 6% in year ending (YE) June 2026 (to 48,615 offences), compared with YE June 2025 (51,567 offences). Levels remained 12% lower than YE March 2020 (55,170 offences).
And, on shoplifting, the Tories are again presenting the data in a misleading way. The ONS says:
Following a period of increases in shoplifting, there has been a 2% decrease (to 519,516 offences) in YE June 2026 when compared with the previous year (530,336 offences).
The Tories have justified their “record high” claim by combining the shoplifing figures with the figures for robberies from business properties. They describe this as “shop crime” – even though many business properties are not shops. And the ONS has a caveat about these figures too.
The number of robbery of personal property offences fell by 7% (to 57,193 offences) compared with the previous year, however, overall robbery increased by 10% (to 88,282 offences) mainly because of improvements to recording practices for robbery of business property.
And the ONS says, with shoplifting, more offences are also now being recorded than in the past.
Recent increases in police recorded shoplifting likely reflect both growth in offences and improved reporting resulting from closer engagement between police and retailers. Reporting rates for shoplifting are known to be very low and police are actively encouraging the reporting of all incidents and the submission of supporting evidence, such as CCTV, to strengthen intelligence, identify offenders, and link related offences.
